idiom_name: std::sync::Barrier::wait() (reusable) + Barrier/Condvar/mpsc for the one-shot latch
implementation_notes: std::sync::Barrier is the reusable rendezvous: wait() blocks the caller until the configured number of threads have arrived and returns a BarrierWaitResult whose is_leader() designates exactly one participant for phase-local work; the barrier is reusable after every generation. There is deliberately no std::latch, so the one-shot fan-in is expressed as Barrier::new(n + 1) with the collector as the extra party, as a Mutex plus Condvar counter, or as an mpsc channel drained n times; when no phases are involved, std::thread::scope already joins its threads and is the simplest correct form. Blocking waits belong on OS threads - inside an async runtime they stall a runtime worker, so async code should use its runtime's own barrier instead.
pitfalls: A panicking thread leaves the remaining parties blocked forever: Barrier has no timeout and no broken state, so a failure policy (an AtomicBool checked after each wait, or an explicit cancellation channel) is mandatory when workers may fail.
The party count is fixed at construction and must equal the number of waiters: spawning one thread too few blocks the group, and one too many releases a generation with a participant missing.
std::sync::Barrier::wait blocks the OS thread; calling it from an async executor's worker thread (or inside a Future poll) starves other tasks - use the runtime's own barrier in async code.
A thread that has already returned cannot participate: a loop that joins workers between phases and re-spawns them must also re-create the barrier, because generations and threads must match.
